cd /Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/git-sync
gh pr create --base main --head soph/security-bounds-and-redaction \
  --title "Bound remote-declared sizes, quote SSH paths, redact URL credentials" \
  --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Six findings from a full security review of the codebase. All localized, all independently testable. The four findings that need a design call are deliberately **not** here — see the bottom.

Companion PR #106 handles the dependency/toolchain half.

## 1. A packfile header can request an unbounded allocation — *critical*

`internal/gitproto/commitparents.go` sized its per-object buffer from the size the pack header **declares**, before reading any content. go-git validates only that the size varint doesn't overflow, so the value is remote-controlled up to `int64`.

A 48-byte packfile:

```
--- declared size=131072 GiB, pack bytes=48
runtime: out of memory: cannot allocate 140737488355328-byte block
fatal error: out of memory

runtime.makeslice(...)
gitproto.(*commitParentsStorer).RawObjectWriter(0x…, 0x1, 0x800000000000)
    internal/gitproto/commitparents.go:112
```

That's a Go **fatal error**, not a panic — `recover()` can't contain it, so an embedding service dies with the process. A 46-byte pack declaring 64 GiB allocated 64 GiB (measured `TotalAlloc`). Reachable from ordinary planning: `FetchCommitParents` runs against the source for ancestry checks.

Now rejected above 64 MiB — this path only reads `tree:0`-filtered packs, whose objects are commits and tags measured in kilobytes — and otherwise used only to size the initial buffer, capped at 64 KiB, so allocation tracks bytes actually received rather than bytes a remote claims it will send.

## 2. Command injection via the tilde exemption in SSH path quoting — *high*

The remote command string is interpreted by the remote login shell. `shellQuotePath` exempted everything before the first slash when the path began with `~`, so the shell would expand it. A SCP-style URL puts attacker-influenceable text exactly there:

```
git@host:~a;id/repo.git   →   git-upload-pack ~a;id/'repo.git'
```

`id` runs on the remote host as the authenticated SSH user. This matters wherever only *part* of the URL is caller-controlled — a repository path templated into a fixed host, or one arriving from a webhook or config.

Quoting the whole path is free: `~` expansion doesn't depend on the shell here, because `git-upload-pack` resolves the path through `enter_repo()`, which interpolates a leading `~` itself. Canonical git quotes the whole path for the same reason.

The regression test runs the generated command through a real `/bin/sh` against a stubbed `git-upload-pack` and asserts the path arrives as one literal argument with no injected command executed. Confirmed to fail against the pre-fix code:

```
--- FAIL: TestSSHRemoteCommandSurvivesShellInterpretation/git@example.com:~`id`/repo.git
    injected command ran: "git-upload-pack ~`id`/'repo.git'" executed `id`
```

## 3. URL-embedded credentials echoed to output — *medium*

`probe` and `fetch` carried `Source.URL`/`Target.URL` verbatim into results that print to stdout and serialize into `--json`, so the standard CI form `REDACTED` put the token where automation collects and stores it. Two error paths leaked it as well: `url.Parse` embeds the raw URL in its message, and net/http masks only the *password*, leaving a token in the **username** position — the form GitHub App and PAT URLs normally take.

New `internal/redact` package strips the entire userinfo component. `httpError` moves off `url.URL.Redacted()` for the same reason. This generalizes the helper `convert-sha256` already had (its unparseable-URL placeholder changes from `<source url redacted>` to `<url redacted>`).

Verified against the built CLI:

```
$ git-sync probe --source-url "REDACTED" --json
{ "sourceUrl": "http://host/repo.git", … }

$ git-sync probe --source-url "http://ghp_TOKEN@127.0.0.1:1/repo.git"
error: … request info-refs: http://127.0.0.1:1/repo.git/info/refs?…: dial tcp …: connection refused
```

## 4–5. Unbounded reads — *low*

- **Advertisements.** HTTP capped `/info/refs` at 64 MiB; SSH used a bare `io.ReadAll` and the remote-helper transport accumulated pkt-lines until a flush a remote need never send. All three now share one `MaxAdvertisementBytes` ceiling.
- **Pack spill.** `ExtractCommitParents` copies a non-seekable pack to a temp file for the parser, previously with no limit — a source could fill the disk during what is only a planning round trip. Capped at 4 GiB.

## 6. Workflow permissions — *low*

`permissions: contents: read` on `Tests` and `License Check`, which inherited the repository default while running PR-controlled code (`mise run test:ci`, driven by the PR's own `mise.toml`). `lint.yml` already declared it. Defence in depth, since GitHub already restricts the token for fork PRs — but same-repo branches aren't restricted. I checked the reusable license workflow in `entireio/shared`: it only checks out and runs a mise task, so `contents: read` is sufficient.

## Verification

- `gofmt`, `go vet`, `golangci-lint run` — **0 issues**
- `go test ./...` — 17/17 packages
- `go test -race` on `gitproto`, `redact`, `syncer`
- The SSH and allocation tests were each confirmed to **fail** against the pre-fix code, so they're real regression tests
- Credential redaction checked end to end against the built binary on the success, parse-failure, and connection-failure paths

## Deliberately not in this PR

Each needs a decision rather than a patch:

- **Explicit tokens follow an adopted redirect.** With `--*-follow-info-refs-redirect`, `--source-token`/`--target-token` is re-sent to whatever host the redirect names, *after* Go's stdlib deliberately stripped it on the cross-host hop. Reproduced against a local redirect server. Needs a call on drop-auth vs. refuse-redirect vs. explicit opt-in, plus a doc change — it alters the meaning of a documented flag. The target side leaks a write-scoped token the same way.
- **Ref names from the source are never validated.** Verified: `refs/heads/../../../../tmp/PWNED` writes to `<repo>/tmp/PWNED` during `convert-sha256` (billy clamps at the repo root, so corruption rather than RCE), and a NUL in a ref name lets a source inject capabilities into the push we send to the target. Needs a fail-vs-skip call, since it can start rejecting refs that mirror fine today. #106 hardens the on-disk half upstream.
- **Materialized object limit runs after the memory is spent.** `FetchToStore` fills an in-memory store uncapped, then counts against the 500k limit. The real work is choosing a non-zero `--max-pack-bytes` default, which decides when syncs begin failing.
- **Remote text reaches the terminal and JSON unsanitized** (sideband progress, 64 KiB of HTTP error body, `ng` reasons) — ANSI escape injection. Touches user-visible output.

Plus release-artifact signing and the hand-mirrored `InsecureSkipTLSVerify` flag.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -3

1	# Changelog
2	
3	All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.
4	
5	The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/),
6	and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).
7	
8	## [Unreleased]
9	
10	## [0.8.0] - 2026-07-09
11	
12	### Added
13	
14	- `gitsync.SetIdentity(service, version)` — lets an embedding service name itself in every request git-sync makes. The HTTP User-Agent and the git-protocol `agent=` capability become `<service>/<version> git-sync/<git-sync-version> go-git/<go-git-version>` (non-git provider requests carry the same string without the go-git token). Previously an embedder had no way to identify itself: the advertised version lives in an internal package, and the old doc comment claiming "SDK consumers may overwrite it" was unimplementable from outside the module.
15	
16	- `RefScope.ExcludeRefs` — exact ref-name exclusion, alongside the existing prefix-based `ExcludeRefPrefixes`. An excluded exact name is not pulled, pushed, or pruned, but — unlike a prefix — its children are unaffected, so a caller can reserve a directory-anchor ref like `refs/heads/entire` while still mirroring `refs/heads/entire/foo`. Threaded through `RefScope` → planner `PlanConfig`; `IsRefExcluded` now takes both prefix and exact lists.
17	
18	### Changed
19	
20	- The default advertised git-sync version is now resolved from the binary's embedded build info instead of the hardcoded `"dev"`: embedders automatically advertise the git-sync module version they built against, and a `go install ...@version` CLI build advertises that version. `"dev"` remains only for builds with no usable version (e.g. a plain `go build` of this repo). The goreleaser-stamped CLI version still takes precedence when present.
21	
22	### Removed
23	
24	- The built-in Entire DB credential store integration (`hosts.json` active-user lookup, the file/keyring token store, and OAuth refresh-token handling). `auth.Resolve` now resolves only explicit token/bearer credentials; everything else defers to the git credential helper on a 401, exactly as for any other remote. The Entire mirroring pipeline and the `git-remote-entire` helper already supply credentials directly (installation / repo-scoped tokens at the transport layer), so nothing produced the `hosts.json`/token-store layout this code read. This drops the `github.com/zalando/go-keyring` dependency and, with the file token store gone, the package now compiles on Windows without a `flock` shim.
25	
26	### Fixed
27	
28	- Concurrent **create** races on the target are now classified as `ErrTargetRefMoved`, matching the existing concurrent-update handling. entire-server rejects a create command (old = zero hash) for a ref that already exists with `already exists`; git-sync only plans a create for a ref it found absent at plan time, so that rejection is an unambiguous benign race — a second sync of the same repo created the ref first — exactly like the update-side `remote ref has changed`. Previously only the update reason was in `concurrentMoveMarkers`, so a create race fell through as a generic push failure and `errors.Is(err, ErrTargetRefMoved)` returned false; embedders that key redelivery/alerting off the sentinel (e.g. mirror-pipeline's worker) misclassified it as a hard sync failure. Both the create and update CAS rejections now satisfy `errors.Is(err, ErrTargetRefMoved)`.
29	
30	## [0.7.0] - 2026-06-16
31	
32	### Added
33	
34	- Typed push-rejection errors on the public API. `Sync`/`Replicate` now report a `*RefRejectedError` (carrying the rejected `Ref` and the raw server `Reason`) for per-ref receive-pack `ng` statuses, reachable with `errors.As`. Rejections that are unambiguous concurrent target-ref moves — entire-server's compare-and-swap rejection (`remote ref has changed`) and git's `--force-with-lease` lease miss (`stale info`) — additionally satisfy `errors.Is(err, ErrTargetRefMoved)`. This lets embedders distinguish a benign racing concurrent push (retryable) from a genuine push failure without substring-matching the free-form error message. Ambiguous markers (`non-fast-forward` / `fetch first`) are deliberately excluded from the move classification so a real "needs `--force`" rejection is not masked. The `ForceWithLease` lease-failure escalation (raised even under `BestEffort`) also satisfies `errors.Is(err, ErrTargetRefMoved)`, though it is not itself a `*RefRejectedError` — prefer `errors.Is` over `errors.As` when you only need the cause. The error message and the underlying value-typed `packp.CommandStatusErr` are preserved unchanged (reach it with a value `errors.As` target), so existing checks keep working ([#71](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/71))
35	
36	### Fixed
37	
38	- Concurrent target-ref rejections are now actually classified — `errors.Is(err, ErrTargetRefMoved)` and `errors.As(err, *RefRejectedError)` match on the real push path. go-git returns `packp.CommandStatusErr` **by value** from `ReportStatus.Error()`, but `asRefRejectedError` / `annotateLeaseFailure` used a `*packp.CommandStatusErr` (pointer) `errors.As` target, which never matches a value in the chain — so every live receive-pack `ng` status passed through unclassified and `ErrTargetRefMoved` was never reported. Both now use a value target, and a regression test drives a real `ReportStatus.Error()` end to end so a pointer-vs-value relapse fails CI. (Bug in the typed-rejection feature above — never shipped in a tagged release.) ([#73](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/73))
39	- Batched bootstrap no longer dies when finalizing a subsumed branch against a receive-pack that requires a pack for every non-delete command. The pack-less ref-create sent only command pkt-lines, which strict servers rejected with `unpack error: ... read packfile header: EOF` (observed mid-run mirroring to entiredb prod, leaving the target half-populated); git-sync now sends a valid empty pack with such creates ([#74](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/74))
40	- Large or slow bootstrap relays that outlast the target's `git-receive-pack` deadline (GitHub HTTP 408, or gateway 504) now fall back to batched bootstrap with checkpoint subdivision instead of hard-failing. Previously only 413 body-limit rejections triggered batching, so relaying a large repo over a slow source link — where the upstream read rate throttles the downstream write past GitHub's receive-pack window — failed with a bare `http 408` and no remediation. Timeouts are classified distinctly from size rejections, the auto-batch notice names the cause, and a one-shot failure with no batched fallback (source lacking protocol-v2 fetch-filter support) now carries actionable guidance ([#75](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/75))

46	- `git-sync convert-sha256`: one-off conversion that fetches a pack over smart HTTP from a SHA1 source, walks every reachable object via a two-pass topological DFS, and writes a fresh SHA256 bare repository with every tree/commit/tag reference re-encoded — including abbreviated SHA1 prefixes in commit messages. All branches and tags are always converted to avoid stranding cross-branch references; sharp edges and operational characteristics are documented in `docs/convert-sha256.md` ([#66](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/66))

## [#107 — six code findings](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/107)

| # | Fix |
|---|---|
| 01 | Declared pack-object size bounded at 64 MiB, prealloc capped at 64 KiB |
| 03 | `shellQuotePath` deleted — SSH paths quoted in full |
| 04 | New `internal/redact` package applied to results + all three error paths |
| 08 | Shared `MaxAdvertisementBytes` across HTTP, SSH, and helper transports |
| 09 | Commit-graph temp spill capped at 4 GiB |
| 12 | `permissions: contents: read` on two workflows |

586 insertions / 89 deletions, ~250 of it production code. `gofmt`, `go vet`, `golangci-lint` (0 issues), `go test ./...` 17/17, `-race` on the touched packages.

Two things worth flagging from doing the work:

**The regression tests were verified to fail against the old code.** I temporarily restored the vulnerable tilde quoting and confirmed the SSH test catches actual exploitation: `injected command ran: "git-upload-pack ~`id`/'repo.git'" executed `id``. The test drives the generated command through a real `/bin/sh` against a stubbed `git-upload-pack`, so it asserts the property that matters rather than a string shape.

**Finding 04 was bigger than my report said, in one direction and smaller in another.** Smaller: the sync `Result` has no URL fields, so the echo surface is only `probe` and `fetch` — I'd implied it was broader. Bigger: I'd noted the error path "masks the password but not the username," and that turned out to be *two* separate paths — `httpError` for non-2xx responses, and `http.Client.Do` transport failures (connection refused, DNS, TLS) which never reach `httpError` at all. Both are now covered; I verified against the built binary that no token survives on the success, parse-failure, or connection-failure path.

Two housekeeping notes: your disk was at 100% (926Gi full) and blocked me mid-task — **68GB of it was an accumulated Go build cache**, which I cleared with `go clean -cache`; builds will be slower once until it repopulates. And `redactSourceURL`'s unparseable-URL placeholder changed from `<source url redacted>` to `<url redacted>` now that it's shared; it's noted in the CHANGELOG in case anything greps for it.

The four findings needing a design call (redirect-token leak, ref-name validation, materialized limit default, output sanitization) are written up at the bottom of #107's description so they don't get lost. I still have the two-server redirect harness if you want it as the regression test when you decide how to handle that one.

func newSSHShimEnv(t *testing.T) sshShimEnv {
	t.Helper()
	dir := t.TempDir()
	logFile := filepath.Join(dir, "ssh.log")
	countFile := filepath.Join(dir, "count")
	bodyPrefix := filepath.Join(dir, "body-")
	script := filepath.Join(dir, "ssh-shim.sh")
	content := strings.Join([]string{
		"#!/bin/sh",
		"count=0",
		"if [ -f " + shellQuote(countFile) + " ]; then count=$(cat " + shellQuote(countFile) + "); fi",
		"count=$((count+1))",
		"printf '%s' \"$count\" >" + shellQuote(countFile),
		"dest=\"\"",
		"remote=\"\"",
		"port=\"\"",
		"if [ \"$1\" = \"-o\" ]; then",
		"  shift 2",
		"fi",
		"if [ \"$1\" = \"-p\" ]; then",
		"  port=\"$2\"",
		"  shift 2",
		"fi",
		"if [ \"$1\" = \"--\" ]; then",
		"  shift",
		"fi",
		"if [ -n \"$port\" ]; then",
		"  dest=\"-p $port $1\"",
		"else",
		"  dest=\"$1\"",
		"fi",
		"remote=\"$2\"",
		"printf '%s\\t%s\\n' \"$dest\" \"$remote\" >>" + shellQuote(logFile),
		"cat >" + shellQuote(bodyPrefix) + "\"$count\"",
		"printf 'response-%s' \"$count\"",
	}, "\n")
	if err := os.WriteFile(script, []byte(content), 0o755); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("write ssh shim: %v", err)
	}

name: no-unfixed-vulns-in-public-prs
description: Never put details of unfixed vulnerabilities in public PR bodies, issues, or commit messages
metadata:

When fixing some security findings but not others, keep the unfixed ones out of
anything public. On 2026-08-19 I listed four unfixed findings — including a
reproduced credential-exfiltration vector — in a "Deliberately not in this PR"
section of a PR description on `entireio/git-sync`, which is a **public** repo.
Soph removed the section and told me those "should have been not disclosed yet."

**Why:** a public PR body is disclosure. Naming an unfixed vector with enough
detail to reproduce it hands it to anyone reading, before a fix exists — the
opposite of what the repo's own [[SECURITY.md]] policy asks of reporters.
Describing findings that the same PR *fixes* is fine and normal; the line is
whether a fix has landed.

**How to apply:** check repo visibility (`gh repo view --json visibility`)
before writing any security-related PR or issue. In public artifacts, describe
only what the change fixes. Refer to remaining work without specifics — "further
findings are tracked privately" — and put the detail somewhere private: a draft
GitHub security advisory, a private tracker, or a direct message. This applies
to PR bodies, issue text, commit messages, and review replies.

You were right to pull that section — and it was a worse slip than just #107.

## The disclosure

I'd put the same "four unfixed findings" detail in **#106's** description too, including the reproduced credential-exfiltration vector. I've removed it and replaced it with a neutral pointer:

> Further findings from the review are tracked privately and will be handled separately.

I verified the repo is `PUBLIC`, then checked the rest of the trail: #107's body is clean after your edit, and neither branch's commit messages name an unfixed issue — they describe only what the commits fix, which is normal practice. I've written this down as a durable rule so I check visibility before writing anything security-related, rather than relying on remembering.

One thing still holding the full set: the audit artifact from earlier. It's private by default and only you can share it, but it contains all thirteen findings with reproductions — worth keeping unshared until the rest land. If it'd help, I can produce a fixed-only version that's safe to circulate, and put the remaining four in a draft GitHub security advisory (private, and it converts to a CVE request if you ever want one).

## Bugbot found a real regression — mine

Its comment was correct, and it caught something my own tests missed. Bounding the advertisement read stopped the memory growth but left the far side still writing, so I'd **traded an OOM for a deadlock**. I reproduced both before fixing:

- **SSH** — hung the full 30s. `cmd.wait()` was called with stdout still open, so the writer filled the pipe and never exited.
- **Remote helper** — hung the full 60s, in `finish()`'s unbounded `io.Copy(io.Discard, p.out)`, exactly as described. My cap error never got a chance to surface.

Fixed in `b6d9adfd`: the SSH read-error path closes stdout before waiting (via the existing `cleanupSSHCommand`), and the helper path uses `cleanup()` instead of `finish()` on error, with `finish()`'s drain now bounded at 1 MiB. Both return a limit error in ~1s. Each test was confirmed to fail against the pre-fix code, so they'll catch a relapse. `gofmt`, `vet`, `golangci-lint` (0 issues), 17/17 packages, `-race` clean. I replied to the Bugbot thread with the reproduction details.

Worth saying plainly: I claimed those bounds were verified, and they were — for memory, not for liveness. The lesson is that a resource limit needs a test that the operation still *returns*, not just that it doesn't allocate. I've added exactly that for both transports.

CI hasn't picked up the new commit yet — no runs registered for `b6d9adfd` after several minutes, while the previous commit's runs completed normally. I'm polling in the background and will report. If it stays empty it's likely an Actions queue delay rather than anything in the diff, but you may want to glance at the Actions tab.

### Added

- A `Vulnerability Scan` workflow running `govulncheck ./...` on pull requests, pushes to main, and a weekly schedule. The existing lint suite cannot see this class of issue, and the weekly run matters because advisories are published against versions already in go.mod — without it, a newly disclosed vulnerability goes unreported until someone happens to open a PR.
=======
- **A packfile object header can no longer request an unbounded allocation.** `ExtractCommitParents` sized its per-object buffer from the size the pack header *declares*, before reading any content. go-git validates only that the size varint does not overflow, so the value is remote-controlled up to `int64`: a 48-byte pack declaring a 128 TiB object produced `fatal error: out of memory` — a Go runtime fatal, not a panic, so an embedding process could not contain it with `recover()`. A 46-byte pack declaring 64 GiB allocated 64 GiB. The declared size is now rejected above 64 MiB (this path reads tree:0-filtered packs, whose objects are commits and tags measured in kilobytes) and otherwise only sizes the initial buffer, capped at 64 KiB, so the allocation tracks bytes actually received. Reachable from ordinary planning: `FetchCommitParents` runs against the source during ancestry checks.

- **SSH repository paths are now shell-quoted in full.** The remote command string is interpreted by the remote login shell, and `shellQuotePath` exempted the segment before the first slash when the path began with `~`, so the remote shell would expand it. A SCP-style URL puts attacker-influenceable text in exactly that position: `git@host:~a;id/repo.git` produced the remote command `git-upload-pack ~a;id/'repo.git'`, executing `id` on the remote host as the authenticated SSH user. This matters wherever only part of the URL is caller-controlled — a repository path templated into a fixed host, or a path arriving from a webhook or config. Quoting costs nothing: `~` expansion does not depend on the shell here, because `git-upload-pack` resolves the path through `enter_repo()`, which interpolates a leading `~` itself (canonical git quotes the whole path for the same reason). Regression tests assert the generated command against a real `/bin/sh`.

- **Credentials embedded in a remote URL are no longer echoed.** `probe` and `fetch` carried `Source.URL`/`Target.URL` verbatim into their results, which are printed to stdout and serialized into `--json` — so `REDACTED`, the standard CI form, put the token in output that automation collects. The URL-parse failure path leaked it too, since `url.Parse` embeds the raw URL in its error. All of these now redact the whole userinfo component via the new `internal/redact` package. HTTP error messages switch from `url.URL.Redacted()` to the same helper: `Redacted()` masks only the password, leaving a token in the *username* position (`https://<token>@host/...` — how GitHub App and PAT URLs are normally written) in the clear. The redaction helper that `convert-sha256` already had is what this generalizes; its unparseable-URL placeholder changes from `<source url redacted>` to `<url redacted>`.

- **Advertisement reads are bounded on every transport.** The HTTP path capped `/info/refs` at 64 MiB, but the SSH transport read the advertisement with a bare `io.ReadAll` and the remote-helper transport accumulated pkt-lines until a flush that a remote need never send — either grows until the process dies. All three now share one `MaxAdvertisementBytes` ceiling.

- **The commit-graph pack spill to disk is bounded.** `ExtractCommitParents` copies a non-seekable pack into a temp file to give the parser a seekable source, with no limit on the copy, so a source could fill the disk during what is only a planning round trip. Capped at 4 GiB.

- Added `permissions: contents: read` to the `Tests` and `License Check` workflows, which previously inherited the repository default while running PR-controlled code. `lint.yml` already declared it. The declared size is now rejected above 64 MiB (this path reads tree:0-filtered packs, whose objects are commits and tags measured in kilobytes) and otherwise only sizes the initial buffer, capped at 64 KiB, so the allocation tracks bytes actually received. Quoting costs nothing: `~` expansion does not depend on the shell here, because `git-upload-pack` resolves the path through `enter_repo()`, which interpolates a leading `~` itself (canonical git quotes the whole path for the same reason). questions.question: For the redirect leak: when /info/refs redirects to a different host and --*-follow-info-refs-redirect is on, what should happen to an explicit --source-token / --target-token?

options.label: Same-site only, else drop (Recommended)
options.description: Forward the token when the redirect target is the same host or a subdomain of the one you typed (Go's own rule for retaining auth headers); drop it otherwise and fall back to the credential helper. Keeps github.com → codeload.github.com style replicas working. Breaks a replica on a genuinely different domain (e.g. *.githubusercontent.com).

options.label: Explicit host allowlist
options.description: New --source-redirect-allow-host / --target-redirect-allow-host flags. The token goes only to hosts you name; empty allowlist means drop. Safest and most explicit, but every deployment using the flag today needs config added or it starts 401ing.

options.label: Bind token to typed host only
options.description: Closest to vanilla git: the explicit token is only ever sent to the host you typed. Cross-host redirect targets get the credential helper or nothing. Simplest to reason about, but any replica needing the same token breaks unless operators add a helper entry.

options.label: Refuse cross-host redirects
options.description: Fail the run with a clear error rather than silently changing hosts. Fails closed and is trivially auditable, but turns a working-today configuration into a hard error.

questions.question: For ref names from the source that fail validation (containing .., control characters, NUL, or a leading dash) — what should git-sync do?

options.label: Skip the ref, warn, continue (Recommended)
options.description: Matches the existing BestEffort model where per-ref problems become warnings. A mirror doesn't halt because upstream has one malformed ref, and the operator sees it in output. Downside: the mirror silently diverges from source for that ref unless someone reads the warning.

options.label: Fail the whole run
options.description: Any invalid ref name aborts. Strongest integrity guarantee and impossible to miss, but one malformed upstream ref stops all mirroring — and you'd find out in production rather than at review time.

options.label: Fail for convert-sha256, skip+warn for sync
options.description: Split by risk: writing to disk (where a bad name escapes refs/) fails hard, while remote-to-remote mirroring warns and continues. More code paths to reason about, but matches where the actual danger is.

Bind explicit credentials to the host they were configured for

With --source-follow-info-refs-redirect / --target-follow-info-refs-redirect,
git-sync adopts the host /info/refs redirected to and addresses it
directly for the follow-up RPCs — and re-attached the configured token to
those requests, after Go's http.Client had deliberately stripped the
Authorization header on the cross-host hop. Any redirect an attacker
could cause collected the token: an open redirect on the real host, a
hostile mirror, or a man-in-the-middle on a plain-http source. On the
target side that token usually carries write access.

An explicitly supplied credential — token flags, bearer flags, or
userinfo in the URL — is now sent only to the host named on the command
line and its subdomains, on the same scheme and port. Anything else gets
nothing, plus a warning naming the withheld host, and the credential
helper is consulted for that host instead. Credentials resolved *from*
the helper are untouched: those are looked up keyed on the host actually
being challenged, so they were already bound to their destination.

The same-site rule is deliberately stricter than the stdlib's. Go
compares hostnames only, ignoring scheme and port, so it will carry
Authorization from host:443 to host:9999 — a different service, and on
shared infrastructure potentially a different tenant. That gap is not
visible from the request-building code either, because the redirect is
followed inside a single http.Client.Do: by the time control returns the
header is already on the wire. So redirect policy moves into a
per-connection CheckRedirect that strips the header on any hop leaving
the endpoint's site, layered over whatever policy the caller set. Setting
CheckRedirect replaces the stdlib's ten-redirect default, so that cap is
reimposed explicitly rather than lost.

The subdomain allowance keeps the case the flag exists for working: a
hosting replica under the same domain, example.com to
replica.example.com, still authenticates.

Tests cover the rule in isolation (including the near-misses: suffix
without a dot boundary, attacker-controlled prefix domain, scheme
downgrade, port change, IP addresses having no subdomains) and end to end
against httptest servers, asserting the cross-site POST carries no
credentials while a same-site redirect still does. Verified by hand too:
the original two-server reproduction that leaked the token now logs an
empty Authorization on both requests to the redirect target.

docs/usage.md gains a "Credentials and redirects" section — the flags
were previously documented only in their flag help.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git push -q -u origin soph/security-bind-token-to-host 2>&1 | tail -2
gh pr create --base soph/security-bounds-and-redaction --head soph/security-bind-token-to-host \
  --title "Bind explicit credentials to the host they were configured for" \
  --body "$(cat <<'BODY'
Fixes the highest-severity item left from the security review. **Stacked on #107** so the `smarthttp.go` changes don't conflict — the base is that branch, so this diff shows only its own changes. I'll rebase onto `main` once #107 merges.

## The problem

With `--source-follow-info-refs-redirect` / `--target-follow-info-refs-redirect`, git-sync adopts the host `/info/refs` redirected to and addresses it directly for follow-up RPCs — re-attaching the configured token to requests aimed at that host, *after* Go's `http.Client` had deliberately stripped `Authorization` on the cross-host hop.

Reproduced with two local servers, where the endpoint 307s to an unrelated host:

```
[LEGIT] GET  Authorization="Basic Z2l0OlNVUEVSX1NFQ1JFVF9QQVRfMTIzNDU="
[EVIL]  GET  Authorization=""                    ← stdlib stripped it
[EVIL]  POST Authorization="Basic Z2l0OlNVUEVS…" ← git-sync re-sent it
```

Any redirect an attacker can cause is enough: an open redirect on the real host, a hostile mirror, or a MITM on a plain-`http` source. On the target side the token usually carries write access.

## The fix

An explicitly supplied credential — token flags, bearer flags, or userinfo in the URL — now goes only to the host named on the command line and its subdomains, on the same scheme and port. Anything else gets nothing, plus a warning naming the withheld host, and the credential helper is consulted for that host instead:

```
source: withholding the configured credentials from http://localhost:64772/repo.git:
/info/refs redirected outside 127.0.0.1. Consulting the git credential helper for that host instead.
```

Credentials resolved *from* the helper are untouched — they're looked up keyed on the host being challenged, so they were already bound to their destination. The subdomain allowance keeps the case the flag exists for working: `example.com` → `replica.example.com` still authenticates.

## Why redirect policy moved into git-sync

The same-site rule is stricter than the stdlib's on purpose. Go compares hostnames only, ignoring scheme and port, so it forwards `Authorization` from `host:443` to `host:9999` — a different service, potentially a different tenant. My first version of the end-to-end test caught exactly this: both `httptest` servers are on `127.0.0.1`, so the stdlib happily carried the token across the port boundary and the test failed.

That hop isn't visible from the request-building code, because the redirect is followed *inside* a single `http.Client.Do`. So policy now lives in a per-connection `CheckRedirect` that strips the header on any hop leaving the endpoint's site, layered over whatever policy the caller set (theirs still runs and can still veto). Setting `CheckRedirect` replaces the stdlib's ten-redirect default, so that cap is reimposed explicitly — otherwise this fix would have introduced a redirect-loop hang.

The client is shallow-copied per connection, sharing the caller's `Transport`, so nothing the caller passed in is mutated or reconfigured.

## Tests

- `sameSite` in isolation, including the near-misses: suffix without a dot boundary (`notgithub.com` vs `github.com`), attacker-controlled prefix domain (`github.com.evil.example`), scheme downgrade, port change, and IP addresses having no subdomains.
- End to end against `httptest`: the cross-site POST must carry no credentials, and a same-site redirect must still carry them.
- By hand: the original two-server reproduction now logs an empty `Authorization` on both requests to the redirect target.

`gofmt`, `go vet`, `golangci-lint` (0 issues), `go test ./...` 17/17, `-race` on `gitproto` and `syncer`.

## Behavior change to be aware of

If a deployment today relies on the redirect target receiving the configured token and that target is **not** same-site with the endpoint, it will start getting 401s. The fix is to store those credentials in the git credential helper against the redirect host — git-sync will find them there. `docs/usage.md` gains a "Credentials and redirects" section explaining this; the flags were previously documented only in their flag help text.

Nothing checked the names a remote advertises, and git-sync acts on them
in two ways that make a malformed one dangerous.

the repository filesystem, so "refs/heads/../../config" escapes

line, so a source advertising a name containing NUL can inject
capabilities into the push git-sync sends to the target.

git's check_refname_format: "..", NUL, CR, LF, other control characters,
DEL, space, "~^:?*[", backslash, "@{", a ".lock" suffix, a leading dot,
empty components, and a leading dash on a branch or tag. Deferring rather
than hand-rolling keeps git-sync's notion of a valid ref identical to
git's, so nothing git considers legitimate gets skipped — verified
against refs/pull/*, refs/notes/*, and nested branch names.

Third of the remaining security-review items. **Stacked on #108** (which is stacked on #107); base is that branch so the diff shows only this change. Merge order: #107 → #108 → this.

## Why it matters

Nothing validated the names a remote advertises, and git-sync acts on them in two places where a malformed name bites:

**Written to disk.** `convert-sha256` passes advertised names to `SetReference`, and go-git resolves a name through the repository filesystem. Verified against go-git: `refs/heads/../../../../tmp/PWNED` lands at `<repo>/tmp/PWNED`, and `refs/heads/sub/../../../PWNED2` at `<repo>/PWNED2`. go-billy clamps traversal at the repository root, so this is repository corruption rather than arbitrary file write — but `config`, `HEAD`, and `packed-refs` are all reachable, with content constrained to an object hash.

**Embedded in receive-pack commands.** go-git's `formatCommand` writes the name verbatim, and receive-pack reads a feature list from everything after the first NUL on a command line. So a source advertising a name containing NUL injects capabilities into the push git-sync sends to *your* target.

`govulncheck` also flagged this call site under **GO-2026-6214**; #106 took the upstream fix, but validating at the trust boundary is git-sync's own job and also covers the push side, which the upstream fix does not.

## Approach

Validation defers to `plumbing.ReferenceName.Validate` — go-git's implementation of git's `check_refname_format`. I checked its coverage empirically before relying on it; it rejects `..`, NUL, CR, LF, other control characters, DEL, space, `~^:?*[`, backslash, `@{`, a `.lock` suffix, a leading dot, empty components, and a leading dash on a branch or tag. Deferring rather than hand-rolling keeps git-sync's notion of a valid ref identical to git's, so nothing git accepts gets skipped — confirmed against `refs/pull/*`, `refs/notes/*`, and nested branch names.

It runs at the two **decode boundaries** (`AdvRefsToSlice`, `decodeV2LSRefs`) rather than at each call site, so every path that reads an advertisement is covered by construction — source and target both. A skipped target ref is also one the planner never sees, so it's never picked as a prune candidate: the safe direction.

## Skip vs fail

Advertised names are **skipped with a warning**, matching how per-ref push rejections behave under `BestEffort` — one malformed ref upstream shouldn't stop a mirror. The warning names what was dropped so the divergence isn't silent, prints names with `%q` (they're remote-controlled, and an embedded escape sequence would otherwise reach the terminal), and caps the individual list while the count still covers everything.

`--map` values get the same validation but are **rejected outright**. They're configuration, and a mapped target ref reaches the same places an advertised one does, so failing at startup beats silently not mirroring what was asked for. Note this also closes the short-name form, where `--map main:../../config` becomes `refs/heads/../../config` after the prefix is added.

## Tests

- Every dangerous shape is covered individually with the reason it matters: parent traversal, traversal mid-path, NUL feature-list smuggling, CR, LF, ANSI escape, leading dash, `.lock` suffix, `@{0}`. Each asserts the *valid* ref alongside it still survives.
- Legitimate names must not regress: nested branches, tags, `refs/notes/commits`, `refs/pull/42/head`, `refs/merge-requests/7/head`.
- The warning must not leak raw control characters, must truncate, and must count everything.
- Mapping validation, including the short-name path.

## Behavior change to be aware of

If a source currently advertises a ref name git would reject, that ref stops being mirrored and a warning names it. Previously it would have been attempted and — depending on the target — either rejected server-side or written somewhere unintended.

Fourth of the remaining security-review items. **Stacked on #109**; merge order is #107 → #108 → #109 → this.

## The problem

`FetchToStore` filled the in-memory store with no cap. The object limit — `--materialized-max-objects`, default 500,000 — was checked against the object *closure* once the fetch had already finished:

```go
hashes, err := e.collectObjectClosure()   // objects are already resident
if err := e.enforceObjectLimit(hashes)    // …and only now do we check
```

So it reported an overrun instead of preventing one. The constant's own comment says *"Fail early rather than OOM (issue #15)"*, which the ordering didn't deliver, and README's "guarded by an explicit object-count limit" overstated the protection. `--max-pack-bytes` would have bounded it, but it defaults to `0` and is only wired into the relay and bootstrap paths.

## The fix

The store is wrapped so the count is enforced as objects are decoded, failing the write that would exceed the limit.

`RawObjectWriter` is the choke point, and I verified that rather than assuming it: go-git's pack scanner calls `r.storage.RawObjectWriter(oh.Type, oh.Size)` for every object it decodes (`scanner.go` for non-deltas, `parser.go` for deltas), and memory storage's implementation only reaches `SetEncodedObject` through its own internal `lazyCloser`, which never passes back through the wrapper. So counting in both places would risk double-counting — halving the effective limit — rather than adding coverage.

Reads pass straight through, so planning and the push path see the store exactly as before.

**No new default was needed.** This changes *when* the already-configured, already-documented limit bites, not what it is — which is why it didn't need a product decision about a new byte ceiling.

## Errors

Failures carry an `ErrObjectLimit` sentinel and an `*ObjectLimitError` holding the limit, so callers branch with `errors.Is`/`errors.As` rather than matching message text, and the message names the flag to raise.

The closure check in the materialized strategy stays as a second line of defence, for the case where a closure is large without the fetch itself exceeding the cap.

## Tests

- A 50-object pack decoded into a store bounded at 10: the decode must fail, the error must carry the sentinel and the limit, and the underlying store must hold **no more than the limit** — the property the old ordering could not provide.
- A pack within the limit must decode unchanged, so the guard can't be satisfied by rejecting everything.
- Reads pass through to the underlying store.
- Zero/negative limit returns the input store unwrapped.

The existing integration test asserted the old post-hoc message (`"materialized push requires"`). It now asserts `errors.Is(err, ErrObjectLimit)` plus an actionable message — stronger, and independent of wording. That test failing was the expected signal that the guard had moved.

While tracing the choke point: go-git's `memory` storage `RawObjectWriter` passes the pack-declared size straight to `obj.SetSize(sz)`. The two hardening items from the security review. **Stacked on #110**; merge order is #107 → #108 → #109 → #110 → this.

## Terminal control characters in server-authored text

Five paths carried remote text to terminals, logs and `--json` output unfiltered:

- sideband progress (`prefixedLineWriter`)
- up to 64 KiB of HTTP error body (`httpError`)
- receive-pack `ng` rejection reasons (`RefRejectedError.Reason`, which is serialized into results)
- diagnostic response headers (`Cf-Ray`, `X-Request-Id`, …)
- ssh's relayed `remote:` output (`sshCommandError`)

A hostile remote could embed an escape sequence to redraw the line its own message was printed on — a rejected push made to read like a successful one — or smuggle control characters into whatever ingests the JSON.

All five now go through `internal/sanitize`, which drops everything below `0x20` plus DEL while **keeping** tab, newline and carriage return: git's in-place progress output depends on them, and the `source:`/`target:` line prefix already bounds how much a bare `\r` can hide. Single-byte C1 introducers are deliberately out of scope — in a UTF-8 stream they aren't valid standalone bytes, and terminals in UTF-8 mode don't act on them.

Two details worth noting for review:

- **Classification runs on the raw status.** `isConcurrentMove(cs.Status)` still sees the unfiltered text, so sanitizing cannot change whether a rejection is treated as `ErrTargetRefMoved`.
- **The streaming filter is not a short write.** It reports the byte count it was *given*, not the smaller number written, so `io.Copy` and similar callers don't see an error for text that was intentionally dropped. There's a test for exactly that.

## Deriving the TLS-verification state

`HTTPConn.InsecureSkipTLSVerify` was documented as a field callers must set to match the client they pass in, and the cross-host credential guard reads it:

```go
if c.InsecureSkipTLSVerify && challengeURL.Host != c.requestURL().Host {
```

So a caller who disabled verification on their transport but forgot the field silently lost that protection — the wrong direction for a security check to fail.

The transport is now inspected directly, following `Unwrap` through wrappers so an instrumentation layer can't hide the setting. The syncer's `countingRoundTripper` gained an `Unwrap` for exactly that reason — without it, every syncer-built connection would have been opaque to the check. The walk is bounded so a cyclic chain terminates rather than hanging, and the explicit field still forces the guard on for transports that can't be inspected.

## Tests

- `sanitize.Text`: ESC, OSC, NUL, BEL, backspace, DEL, VT/FF removed; tab/newline/CR kept; multibyte UTF-8 preserved (the filter is byte-oriented, so continuation bytes must survive); plus the concrete line-rewrite spoofing case.
- `sanitize.Writer`: an escape sequence straddling two chunks — the way sideband frames actually arrive — is still caught; all-control input is not a short write; underlying errors propagate.
- TLS detection: bare transport, verification on/off, wrapped once and twice, an opaque wrapper (must report false), and a self-referential cycle (must terminate).
- Both signals on `HTTPConn`: derived from the transport with the field unset, and the explicit field winning when the transport is opaque.

`gofmt`, `go vet`, `golangci-lint` (0 issues), `go test ./...` 18/18, `-race` on `gitproto` and `sanitize`.

## Not covered

`Reason` text is filtered, but a *very* long rejection reason or error body is still passed through at full length (64 KiB for bodies). That's a readability question rather than a safety one, so I left the existing cap alone.

attachment.snippet:
1	![git-sync theme](docs/images/gh-repo-cover.png "git-sync cover image")
2	
3	# git-sync
4	
5	`git-sync` mirrors refs from a source remote to a target remote without creating a local checkout. It uses an in-memory `go-git` object store and talks smart HTTP directly:
6	
7	- `info/refs` ref advertisement for source and target
8	- `upload-pack` fetch from source with target tip hashes advertised as `have`
9	- `receive-pack` push to target with explicit ref update commands and a streamed packfile
10	
11	That keeps the target side incremental without fetching target objects into the local process first.
12	
13	## Why This Exists
14	
15	Mirroring Git data between remotes usually means a local mirror clone followed by a mirror push. That's fine for small repos but turns a remote-to-remote operation into a local storage problem at scale, and shell glue around `git fetch` / `git push` tends to skip planning and structured output.
16	
17	`git-sync` fills that gap. It streams source packs directly into target `receive-pack` when it can, plans every action before pushing, and emits typed JSON for automation.
18	
19	For when to use it (and when not), see [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md).
20	
21	## Commands
22	
23	The main commands are:
24	
25	- `git-sync sync`: mirror source refs into the target
26	- `git-sync replicate`: overwrite target refs to match source via relay, and fail rather than materialize locally
27	
28	`sync` automatically bootstraps an empty target, so the same command covers initial seeding and ongoing sync. To preview what would happen without pushing, run `git-sync plan` — it takes the same flags as `sync`, and `--mode replicate` previews a `replicate` run.
29	
30	For one-off SHA1 → SHA256 repo conversion, `git-sync convert-sha256` fetches from an HTTP source and writes a new SHA256 bare repo on disk, with optional commit-message hash rewrites, an origin-notes ref, and a sidecar mapping file. See [docs/convert-sha256.md](docs/convert-sha256.md).
31	
32	For command examples, JSON output, auth, protocol flags, and advanced command notes, see [docs/usage.md](docs/usage.md).
33	
34	## Library API
35	
36	`git-sync` is also a Go library. Use `entire.io/entire/git-sync` for the stable embedding surface (`Probe`, `Plan`, `Sync`, `Replicate`, typed results, auth and HTTP injection). `entire.io/entire/git-sync/unstable` exposes advanced controls (`Bootstrap`, `Fetch`, batching knobs, heap measurement) and is not stable.
37	
38	## Installation
39	
40	### Homebrew (macOS, Linux)
41	
42	```bash
43	brew tap entireio/tap
44	brew install --cask git-sync
45	```
46	
47	### `go install`
48	
49	Requires Go 1.26 or newer.
50	
51	```bash
52	go install entire.io/entire/git-sync/cmd/git-sync@latest
53	```
54	
55	This drops a `git-sync` binary into `$(go env GOPATH)/bin`. Make sure that directory is on your `PATH`.
56	
57	### From source
58	
59	```bash
60	git clone https://github.com/entireio/git-sync.git
61	cd git-sync
62	go build -o git-sync ./cmd/git-sync
63	```
64	
65	### Verifying a download
66	
67	Release archives and `checksums.txt` carry signed build provenance tied to this
68	repository and the workflow that produced them. Check a download before running
69	it:
70	
71	```bash
72	gh attestation verify git-sync_<version>_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz --repo entireio/git-sync
73	```
74	
75	Homebrew verifies the archive checksum from the tap automatically.
76	
77	## Quick Start
78	
79	```bash
80	git-sync sync \
81	  --source-token "$GITSYNC_SOURCE_TOKEN" \
82	  --target-token "$GITSYNC_TARGET_TOKEN" \
83	  https://github.com/source-org/source-repo.git \
84	  https://github.com/target-org/target-repo.git
85	```
86	
87	https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/60adb873-4032-4ab7-b236-24d038e04681
88	
89	## Sync Behavior
90	
91	`sync` picks the bootstrap relay path automatically when the target is empty. For non-empty targets, safe fast-forward updates also use a relay path that streams the source pack directly into target `receive-pack` without local materialization. Anything not relay-eligible (force, prune, deletes, tag retargets) falls back to a materialized path bounded by `--materialized-max-objects`.
92	
93	For branch filtering, ref mapping, tags, pruning, protocol selection, JSON output, and auth details, see [docs/usage.md](docs/usage.md).
94	
95	## Testing
96	
97	Default suite:
98	
99	```bash
100	env GOCACHE=/tmp/go-build go test ./...
101	```
102	
103	Extended and environment-specific test instructions are in [docs/testing.md](docs/testing.md).
104	
105	## Documentation
106	
107	- [docs/usage.md](docs/usage.md) — CLI commands, examples, sync behavior, JSON output, auth, protocol notes
108	- [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md) — product rationale, package layout, operation modes vs transfer modes, memory model
109	- [docs/protocol.md](docs/protocol.md) — smart HTTP, pkt-line, capability negotiation, sideband, relay framing
110	- [docs/convert-sha256.md](docs/convert-sha256.md) — one-off SHA1 → SHA256 repo conversion, mapping outputs, sharp edges
111	- [docs/testing.md](docs/testing.md) — test suites and integration coverage
112	
113	## FAQ
114	
115	### Does it sync complete Git history or only perform a shallow/partial sync?
116	
117	`git-sync` syncs the complete Git object history required for the selected refs. It does not create a shallow clone. Some planning paths may use filtered fetches, but the target receives the full objects needed for valid refs.
118	
119	### Is it just refs, or objects as well?
120	
121	Objects as well. Refs are what `git-sync` plans and updates, but it also transfers the commits, trees, blobs, and tags needed for those refs to exist on the target.
122	
123	### Is it bidirectional?
124	
125	No. `git-sync` is one-way: source remote to target remote. To go the other way you'd run a second invocation with the endpoints swapped.
126	
127	### Does it support create, update, and delete actions?
128	
129	Yes. It supports creating refs, updating refs, force updates with `--force`, and deleting managed refs with `--prune`. `replicate` can overwrite target refs, but it is relay-only and more restrictive than `sync`.
130	
131	### How does it scale?
132	
133	`git-sync` has two transfer paths:
134	
135	- **Relay** — pack data streams from source `upload-pack` directly into target `receive-pack`. The local process holds no object graph, so memory stays bounded regardless of repo size. Used when the target supports relay.
136	- **Materialized fallback** — when relay isn't available, `git-sync` fetches the needed objects into an in-memory `go-git` store, plans, then encodes and pushes a packfile. Memory scales with the diff being pushed and is guarded by an explicit object-count limit. Bootstrap can batch large initial syncs to keep this bounded.
137	
138	Planning itself is cheap: ref-only round-trips, plus a `filter tree:0` fetch for ancestry checks when the source advertises filter support.
139	
140	### How long does it take for a medium-sized repo?
141	
142	It depends on repository size, network speed, and whether the relay path is available. As a rule of thumb, the relay path is bounded by source pack generation + network transfer + target receive-pack time — roughly the time of a `git clone` from the source plus a `git push` of the same pack. The materialized fallback adds local memory work for objects that need inspection.
143	
144	For concrete numbers on your own setup, run the included benchmark tool against a representative repo; see [docs/testing.md](docs/testing.md#benchmarking).
145	
146	### Does it support SSH?
147	
148	Yes. `git-sync` supports SSH remotes through the local `ssh` binary, including
149	`ssh://`, SCP-style `git@host:path.git`, and `git+ssh://` URLs. See
150	[docs/usage.md](docs/usage.md) for details and current caveats.
151	
152	### What about other URL schemes (e.g. `entire://`)?
153	
154	For any scheme it has no native transport for, `git-sync` falls back to a git
155	remote helper named `git-remote-<scheme>` on `PATH`, exactly as `git` does. With

content.text:
All remaining findings now have PRs. The full stack:

| PR | Finding | Severity | CI |
|---|---|---|---|
| [#107](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/107) | allocation bound, SSH quoting, redaction, read caps, permissions | Critical + High + 4 | ✅ |
| [#108](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/108) | explicit tokens bound to their host | High | ✅ |
| [#109](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/109) | ref-name validation | Medium | ✅ |
| [#110](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/110) | object limit enforced while streaming | Medium | ✅ |
| [#111](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/111) | output sanitization + TLS-flag derivation | Low ×2 | ✅ |
| [#112](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/112) | release provenance | Low | running |

Each is stacked on the previous one — `smarthttp.go` and the CHANGELOG's `[Unreleased]` section are touched repeatedly, so branching off `main` would have meant six conflicts. Merge in numeric order and each rebases itself away. #106 is already merged.

Three things from doing the work rather than the review:

**The redirect fix needed more than my report said.** My same-site gate alone wasn't sufficient — my own end-to-end test failed on the first attempt because Go's redirect rule compares *hostnames only*, so it forwarded the token from `127.0.0.1:A` to `127.0.0.1:B` inside a single `Client.Do`, before any code of mine could see it. Redirect policy had to move into a per-connection `CheckRedirect`. That in turn removes the stdlib's ten-redirect cap, so I had to reimpose it or the fix would have introduced a redirect-loop hang.

**Two findings turned out cheaper than estimated.** Ref validation needed no hand-rolled parser — go-git's `ReferenceName.Validate()` already implements `check_refname_format`, and I verified its coverage empirically (`..`, NUL, CR/LF, control chars, `.lock`, `@{`) rather than trusting it. And the object limit needed no new default: enforcing the *existing* 500k limit during the stream instead of after removed the product decision I'd flagged as blocking.

**One test failure was the point.** #110 broke `TestRun_IntegrationMaterializedLimitFailsClearly`, which asserted the old post-hoc message. That failing was the signal the guard had actually moved; I retargeted it at the new `ErrObjectLimit` sentinel, which is stronger than substring-matching anyway.

On verification: everything except #112 is proven by tests that fail against the pre-fix code — I checked that explicitly for the SSH quoting, the allocation bound, both hang fixes, and the token binding. **#112 I could not verify at all**: the release job only runs on a tag push, so nothing in it has executed. The YAML parses and the action SHA is right; the first tagged release is what confirms it. I said so in the PR rather than implying it was tested.

Two loose ends worth your call: Bugbot returned `neutral` (declined to review) on #108 and #110, the two with the most delicate logic — you may want to trigger it manually. And I found an upstream issue while tracing #110: go-git's `memory` storage passes the pack-declared object size straight to `SetSize`, the same remote-controlled value #107 bounds in git-sync's own storer. That's go-git's to fix; I noted it in #110 rather than patching around it, and it's worth reporting to them given you maintain there.

Address review: sanitize what is printed, and drop CR from one-shot text

Two findings from Bugbot, both confirmed against the code.

Sanitizing RefRejectedError.Reason did not change what users see.
Error() returns the wrapped error's message when one is present, which in
production it always is, so the CLI printed the server's raw status:
verified that Reason came out clean while Error() still carried
"\x1b[2K\r". Error() now filters its rendered output, and the non-per-ref
path (an unpack failure, say) is wrapped in a sanitizedError that filters
display while forwarding Unwrap, so errors.Is and errors.As keep matching
exactly what they matched before.

sanitize.Text kept carriage return for git's progress output, but Text is
used on strings that are not progress and not line-prefixed: HTTP bodies,
diagnostic headers, ssh "remote:" text, rejection reasons. A bare CR
rewrites the line without any escape sequence, so "rejected\rok
refs/heads/main" still read as a success. The policy is now split by
entry point: Writer keeps CR, because streamed progress depends on it and
the "source:"/"target:" prefix bounds what a rewritten row can claim;
Text drops it, because a one-shot message has no reason to move the
cursor. The spoofing test asserted only that ESC was gone and so passed
while allowing this — it now checks for both.

Only Bugbot reviewed — no Copilot on any PR. It found **six real issues**, all confirmed and fixed:

## #108 — three findings, one High

**URL userinfo still followed redirects.** The one I'd have been most annoyed to miss. `outgoingAuth` gated `c.Auth`, but `resolvedEndpoint` was `*c.EndpointURL` with only scheme and host replaced — so userinfo came along, and net/http derives Basic auth from `req.URL.User`. I reproduced it before fixing: `Basic dXNlcjpVUkxTRUNSRVQ=` reached the redirect target. Worse than the flag-token case because `outgoingAuth` never sees it, so there was no warning either — a silent leak. Both construction sites now route through one helper that drops userinfo off-site and warns.

**Default ports read as different sites.** A false negative rather than a leak — `https://host` vs `https://host:443` would withhold credentials from a genuinely same-origin replica. Normalized per scheme.

**The warning promised a helper that wasn't installed.** `newConn` only installed the credential helper when `authMethod == nil` — exactly the case where the token *isn't* withheld. So a `--source-token` user hitting a cross-site redirect got a bare 401 and my documented remedy didn't work. The helper is now installed alongside explicit tokens; same-site requests still short-circuit to the token.

## #110 — the object budget

`ensureTagObjects` fetches with `nil` haves into the store the closure already filled, so resent objects were charged twice and a run within the limit could fail. Budget is now per-fetch, reset by `FetchToStore` via an interface. The honest cost, now stated in both the code and the changelog: worst-case residency is limit × number of fetches (two on the sync path). Still bounded, which the original ordering wasn't.

## #111 — two findings, one High

**I sanitized the wrong string.** `Error()` returns the *wrapped* error, which is what the CLI prints:

```
Reason field  : "rejected[2K\rok refs/heads/main"     ← cleaned
Error() output: "…rejected\x1b[2K\rok refs/heads/main" ← what users saw
```

**And `\r` alone is enough to spoof.** My own test passed while allowing it, because it only checked for ESC. The policy is now split: `Writer` keeps `\r` for progress (prefix-bounded), `Text` drops it for one-shot messages that have no reason to move the cursor.

content.content:
Real bug, right fix, and the `sameSite` test table covers the cases that matter. `go vet` and `go test ./...` pass on the branch. Two things I'd change before merge — both are false *negatives* (credentials withheld where they shouldn't be), so they break working setups rather than leak anything.

## 1. `http` → `https` on the same host is now treated as cross-site

`samesite.go:43` requires an exact scheme match, so `sameSite(http://host, https://host)` is `false` (verified directly). A plain-`http` endpoint that redirects to `https` on the same host — GitHub does this, and so does about every corporate reverse proxy — works today, because the stdlib carries `Authorization` when only the scheme changed. After this PR the token is stripped on that hop, and with `--follow-info-refs-redirect` on, `outgoingAuth` then withholds it from every follow-up RPC too. Result: a hard 401 on a config that works today, and the "store it in the credential helper" remedy doesn't apply, because the host didn't change.

The stated goal is "an https endpoint never leaks a token over plaintext http" — that's the *downgrade* direction only. Suggest allowing the upgrade:

```go
if !strings.EqualFold(orig.Scheme, dest.Scheme) &&
	!(strings.EqualFold(orig.Scheme, "http") && strings.EqualFold(dest.Scheme, "https")) {
	return false
}
```

The port normalization already handles 80 → 443. Either way this belongs in the "Behavior change to be aware of" section, which currently mentions only non-same-site *hosts*.

## 2. `guardRedirects` anchors on the user-typed endpoint forever

`smarthttp.go:363` closes over `EndpointURL` at construction, but the connection's effective endpoint moves — `setResolvedEndpoint` adopts the redirect host, and helper credentials are then looked up *for that host*. Any further redirect that never leaves the adopted host still fails `sameSite(EndpointURL, req.URL)` and loses its `Authorization`.
